subject: Re: evasive movements and sample size

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: evasive movements and sample size
parts:
> > Hello all, a couple of questions, kind of new so I apoligize if these questions are obvious. I'm studying a species of grouse and am concerned that some animals move prior to detection and do not flush at all. Histograms of the distances recorded do not highlight evasive movements but perhaps this is because they are holding into the cover or moving beyond the flushing distance. Is there any way to account for this and might this bias my results to the point where the distance technique fails on this particular species??
Yes, if a significant proportion of your birds do this, then the method
will fail - and there is no guarantee that there will be evidence of
this behaviour in the histograms of data. This can be a problem for
gamebirds. It's possible that working a trained dog may reduce the
problem - but it takes a while to train the dog! Another possibility is
if you could estimate the proportion of birds that do this, e.g. by
radio-tagging a few birds, then you could add a correction as a
'multiplier'. Or you could use radio-tagged birds for trials - send an
observer past a bird with known location and note whether the observer
records it. You can estimate a detection function given enough trials
of this type, using say logistic regression. No easy solution I'm afraid.
> >
> >
> > Beyond the issues above, we also have a pretty low encounter rate; we flush about 20 birds per sample season. Am I wrong to want to pool data across years to better model the detection process then use that global detection function to estimate abundance annually? Is this too simplistic or does there need to be statistical justification to pool across years to develop a detection function? My thought is that because survey timing is the same from year to year, w/ the same observers on the same transects, the detection process should be consistent across years. Any thoughts would be greatly appreciated. DAVE
> >
That is easier - yes, you can pool data if you believe the detection
function will be constant. Probably better to test this though, for
example by using the mcds engine of Distance, and entering year as a
factor-type covariate. That allows you to test whether you can assume
the same detection function across years - and provides a means of
estimating different detection functions for each year from the pooled
data, to avoid the small sample size problem.

Steve Buckland
